newsitem.title: USA: Cobalt markets seen heading for rapid oversupply.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt markets seen heading for rapid oversupply.

text.p: The world's cobalt market is accelerating towards oversupply before the end of the decade and prices are set to drop, said Michael Garvey, president of Garvey Associates.
Supply is estimated to rise from 27,000 tonnes in 1996 to 45,000 tonnes by 2005, excluding any U.S. government stockpile sales.
"I don't think there is any doubt cobalt prices will drop and may go through levels that may preclude recycling projects," Garvey said.
Garvey was addressing delegates at the Gorham/Intertech Cobalt Conference in New York Tuesday.
"We are going to be moving to an oversupply situation fairly quickly, with production over 30,000 tonnes by the end of 1998."
"Obviously there is going to have to be new refining capacity built," Garvey said.
"The Cobalt Development Institute will have to spend a few bucks on cobalt development but hopefully there will be an increase in consumption."
Garvey expected Africa to remain the single largest producer, followed by Australia, with extra output from Canada and Cuba, and Russian production remaining level.
Zaire production was due to rise from 9,000 tonnes in 1996 to 10,000 tonnes by 2005.
Zambian production was expected to rise from 3,500 to 5,000 tonnes by 2005.
Garvey doubted whether cobalt recovery from tailings, such as the one owned by Colossal Resources, would be economical at cobalt prices below $20.00 a lb.
Usually cobalt prices need to be at least $15 a lb to obtain a reasonable return in tailings projects, Garvey said.
Cobalt prices surged to almost $30.00 a lb at the start of 1996, plunging to about $18.00 a lb in July, before recovering to about $22 a lb at present.
Australia was expected to produce 10,000 tonnes in 2005, up from 2,900 tonnes at present.
But two tailings projects, Ernest Henry and Mt Isa, could boost output to 24,000 tonnes, by 2005.
Canadian output was set to rise from 3,200 tonnes in 1996 to an estimated 5,900 tonnes in 2005, including the vast Voisey's Bay project, which is due to boost output by 2,700 tonnes.
Garvey noted Voisey's Bay's intention to start up in 1998/99, but added "there is serious doubt that Voisey's Bay will produce any significant quantity prior to 2001."

Garvey said the Canadian Ego group's Cobatec project was disappointing, with capital costs four times the estimate, operating costs "conservatively" twice the estimate and with start up over two years.
"We think current production is still rather small and it is not certain that the project can be economic at low prices," Garvey said.

Cuba's output is due to reach 2,400 tonnes at Moa Bay in 1996, 30 percent above design capacity, due to upgrading by Canada's Sherritt. Output in 1999 is set to reach 4,000-4,500 tonnes, with a further 2,000 tonne rise by 2,005 from Western Mining's Pinares project.
Russia's cobalt output is set to total 4,500 tonnes this year, with 3,000 tonnes at Norilsk, 1,000 tonnes at Severonikel and 500 tonnes custom processed at Yuzuralnikel.
Output at Norilsk and Severonikel will remain at current levels in 2005, with zero output Yuzuralnikel, Garvey said.
--Huw Jones, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1640.
